opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot. Text is an incredibly compressed, human-designed representation. Every token is already a pretty high-level abstraction, because people spent thousands of years evolving language to carry meaning efficiently. So when you train a language model, you're starting from a signal that's already semantically dense. That's a big part of why LLMs got so good so fast.

Pixels are the opposite. They're raw measurements of the physical world. A single image has millions of values, and most of that is redundant or low-level: texture, lighting, noise. The meaning is in there, but it's spread out, and you have to do a lot of work to pull it out. In that sense, a pixel is much less information-dense per unit than a token.

But I don't think that makes pixels less important. If anything it's the other way around. Language is a lossy projection of the world. It's great for communicating ideas between people, but a huge amount of what matters about the physical world never gets written down. Nobody writes a paragraph about exactly how light bounces off a coffee cup, or the precise 3D geometry of a room, but a vision system has to understand those things. So text gives you a shortcut to high-level concepts, and pixels give you grounding in reality.

I also think of it on a scale argument. Text on the internet is finite, and we're getting close to using all the high-quality text there is. Visual data is effectively unbounded. Every camera in the world, every moment, is producing more of it. So in the long run, if you want models that keep getting better and that really understand the world we live in, spatially, physically, in three dimensions, I think you have to learn from pixels, or from richer sensory signals, and not just from language.

So the way I'd weigh them: text is the most efficient way to bootstrap reasoning and abstraction, and pixels are the path to grounding and to understanding the world as it actually is. The interesting work now is figuring out how to bring the two together, so you get the semantic leverage of language with the richness and scale of visual data.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts semantic text with raw pixels, but does not say that tokenizing text loses information about its visual presentation.

r002.rationale: It says pixels provide grounding in the physical world, but does not state that pixels more closely match human visual experience.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss the computational cost of rendering text as an image for a vision model.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is something I think about a lot. The thing about text is that it's already compressed. Language is a lossy, human-designed encoding of the world, and tokenization just chops that encoding into discrete chunks. So when you train an LLM, you're learning over a representation that a few thousand years of human culture already did a lot of work to make dense and meaningful. Every token carries a lot.

Pixels are the opposite. A pixel is basically raw sensor data. A 1024 by 1024 image is a million little measurements, and most of them are redundant. Neighboring pixels are highly correlated, and the actual semantic content of the image, the stuff you'd describe in a sentence, lives in a tiny fraction of that information. So the "bits per unit" is just wildly different between the two modalities.

That's why I don't think it's really fair to compare a token to a pixel directly. The more useful comparison is a token versus a patch, or a token versus a latent code from a VAE or a VQ model. Once you've done that first compression step, you're in a much more comparable regime. And a lot of the interesting modeling decisions in vision are really about where you put that compression. Do you do it with a learned tokenizer up front, like the discrete-token approaches? Do you do it continuously, like latent diffusion? Or do you just throw patches at a transformer and let the model figure out the compression itself, which is kind of the ViT story?

The thing I keep coming back to is that language has a huge advantage in that it's compositional and discrete by construction. The model gets to learn in a space where "a red cube on top of a blue sphere" is a clean sequence of symbols. In pixel space, that same scene is a continuous manifold with lighting, viewpoint, occlusion, and all this nuisance variation baked in. So pixels are much richer, they contain a lot of information that language throws away, but they're also much noisier from the perspective of what you want the model to learn.

And honestly, I think that richness is the whole point. If we only cared about the stuff that language captures, we could just train on captions. The reason to work in pixels, or in 3D, or in video, is precisely that there's structure in the world that no one ever wrote down. The spatial layout, the physics, the fine-grained geometry. The challenge is building representations that keep that structure while getting rid of the redundancy, so the model can actually spend its capacity on the interesting stuff rather than on predicting that the next pixel is probably the same color as the last one.

r001.rationale: The response says language is lossy and that pixels contain information language throws away, but does not clearly state that tokenizing text loses its visual presentation.

r002.rationale: It describes pixels as raw sensor data and discusses visual structure, but does not say pixel representations more closely match human visual experience.

r003.rationale: It does not raise a computational efficiency cost of rendering text as an image for a vision model.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting distinction is how much structure we bake into the representation. With text, we’ve already made this decision that the world is going to be represented as discrete symbols. A tokenizer gives you a sequence that’s relatively compact and useful for predicting what comes next.

Pixels are a much lower-level representation. You have to figure out which pixels belong together, what constitutes an object, and which changes actually matter. Moving an object a few pixels can change a lot of the input without changing the meaning of the scene.

But that’s also what makes pixels exciting: they contain things that are hard to express in language. A description of an image is always throwing information away. So I don’t think it’s a question of which representation wins. It’s how we learn representations that preserve the richness of visual input while giving us some of the abstraction and flexibility that make language so useful.

r001.rationale: The response says tokenization represents text as discrete symbols, but does not state that this loses information about visual presentation.

r002.rationale: The response describes pixels as a low-level representation, but does not say they more closely match human visual experience.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss the computational efficiency cost of rendering text as an image for vision processing.

sol-6.1.text:
I think pixels are a very general representation, but they put a lot of the burden on the model. If I give you a picture of a page of text, you first have to figure out which marks are letters and words before you can reason about what it says. With text tokens, we’ve already done some of that work for you, and that makes the representation much more efficient.

But there’s also information you lose when you turn everything into text. The layout of a page, a diagram, the relationship between a label and an object—those things can matter, and they’re very natural to express visually. So I don’t think it’s necessarily a question of picking one representation for everything. The interesting question is how we build models that can move between them and use whichever representation makes the problem easier.

r001.rationale: It says converting everything into text loses visual information such as page layout and diagram relationships.

r002.rationale: It describes pixels as a general, natural way to express visual information, but does not say they more closely match human visual experience.

r003.rationale: It says a model must identify letters and words in an image before reasoning, while text tokens have already done some of that work, making them more efficient.
